extracted.intended_audience: public administrators and officials in South Africa responsible for making administrative decisions under the Promotion of Administrative Justice Act (AJA)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for administrators on when a decision qualifies as 'administrative action' under the AJA, the procedural fairness duties (sections 3–5), notice-and-comment/public inquiry procedures, requirements for giving reasons, and the grounds/time-limits for judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If an action did not involve a decision, it is not an administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative action requires a decision; mere conduct without a decision does not qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative nature / empowering provision
rubrics_metrics.description: If a decision was taken, it must be of an administrative nature and made in terms of an empowering provision to be administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision must concern how a public function is performed and must have legal authority (an empowering provision such as a statute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the decision is one of the types excluded by the AJA, it is not an administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check section 1 exclusions of the AJA before treating a decision as administrative action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organ of state
rubrics_metrics.description: If the decision is not taken by an organ of state it is (usually) not an administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only actions by organs of state (broadly defined) normally fall under the AJA; private decisions generally do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverse effect on rights
rubrics_metrics.description: If the decision does not adversely affect someone’s rights, it is not an administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative action includes decisions that deprive a person of rights or determine what those rights are (e.g., withdrawing an existing licence, refusing to grant a licence). Rights include constitutional, legislative, contractual or promise-based claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Direct external legal effect' (three components)
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as administrative action, a decision must have a legal effect, the effect must be direct, and it must be external.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal effect: a legally binding determination of rights/obligations or a change/withdrawal of them. Direct effect: the decision must be final — intermediate steps that do not finally affect rights are not directly effective. External effect: the decision must affect someone outside the ordinary internal operations of the organ of state; internal administrative instructions that do not affect individual rights are not administrative action. Examples and explanation provided (suspension of public servant, failing a matric exam vs supervisor instructions or ordinary school test).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical tests (recap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Six practical tests summarising when an action is administrative: decision; administrative nature/empowering provision; not excluded by AJA; taken by organ of state; adversely affects rights; direct external legal effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If any of these are not satisfied, the action will usually not be administrative action under the AJA (though other laws/constitutional requirements may still apply).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness (two parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural fairness comprises (1) consultation / audi alteram partem — the affected person should normally be given an opportunity to tell their side; and (2) absence of bias — the decision-making must be free from real or apparent partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators must give affected persons an opportunity to make representations and must be impartial (justice must be 'done and seen to be done').

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of administrative action requiring procedural fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative action requiring procedural fairness can have either (a) a particular impact (affects rights of a particular individual) or (b) a general impact (affects the public).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular-impact decisions follow Section 3 procedures; general-impact decisions follow Section 4 procedures (e.g., refusing a social pension vs changing pension qualification age).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory procedures (Section 3) — adequate notice of nature and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the decision is taken the affected person must be given adequate notice of the nature and purpose of the proposed administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Adequate notice’ means sufficient time and information for the person to understand what is proposed and why so they can prepare a response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory procedures (Section 3) — reasonable opportunity to make representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the decision is taken the affected person must be given a reasonable opportunity to make representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opportunity should allow objections, new information, or answers to charges; may be written submissions or a hearing depending on circumstances; even if outcome seems unchanged, the opportunity must be given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory procedures (Section 3) — clear statement of the administrative action
rubrics_metrics.description: After the decision is taken the administrator must provide a clear statement of the administrative action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plain language so the affected person understands what has been decided and what will happen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory procedures (Section 3) — adequate notice of right of review or internal appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: After the decision is taken the person must be informed about any right of review or internal appeal including where, when and how to appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators must proactively provide procedural details for internal remedies and review; do not wait for the person to ask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory procedures (Section 3) — adequate notice of right to request reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: After the decision is taken the person must be told of the right to request reasons (where, when, how to request, and where to get assistance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AJA gives a right to written reasons on request; Part 6 explains how to write reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary procedures to consider (Section 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators must consider: providing assistance in responding (e.g., legal representation in serious/complex cases); giving opportunity to present and challenge information; and allowing the person to appear in person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are additional fairness-enhancing procedures — administrators must decide which are fair in the circumstances, though they are not strictly mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 4: decisions affecting the public — choice of public procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When administrative action has a general impact the administrator must decide (mandatory decision) which public procedures to follow: a public inquiry, a notice and comment procedure, or another fair procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The administrator has discretion which of these to use, but must choose and follow a fair procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and comment procedure — four basic steps
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Publish enough information about the proposed action; 2) call for comments and allow enough time; 3) consider the comments received; 4) decide whether to take the action, with or without changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard public participation model for decisions with general impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and comment: draft regulations specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations provide details: notices in Government/Provincial Gazette or local newspaper depending on impact; at least 30 days for comments; notices in English and at least one other official language (chosen appropriately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations change; always check current regulations before running a notice-and-comment procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public inquiry procedure — four basic steps
rubrics_metrics.description: 1) Decide who will conduct the inquiry (self or appointed person/panel); 2) give notice including details/issues; 3) hold a public hearing; 4) compile and publish a written report and summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public inquiry is suited to specific communities/issues or recurring matters; may be used together with notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public inquiry: draft regulations specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations set rules similar to notice-and-comment for notices, provide for assistance to illiterate communities, prescribe notice of hearings (newspapers covering the area), and provide hearing procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult current regulations for detailed procedural requirements and special assistance obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing between notice & comment and public inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment suits decisions with general impact; public inquiry suits matters affecting a specific community or recurring problems; both may be used sequentially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators may also follow other statutory procedures provided they comply with constitutional fairness requirements (section 33).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to give reasons (Part 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally good administrative practice to give reasons for all decisions; under the AJA, a request for reasons must be made within 90 days of awareness and the administrator must give adequate written reasons within 90 days of the request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft reasons when making the decision to facilitate later requests. Reasons given immediately with the decision can help avoid disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who can request reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Anyone whose rights have been adversely affected by administrative action can request written reasons (including persons whose rights were specifically affected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators must be prepared to respond to requests from any adversely affected person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalities of requesting reasons (draft regulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests are generally required to be in writing and sent by post, fax, email or delivered by hand; administrators must assist verbal requesters who cannot write; acknowledge receipt; if refusing to give reasons, inform requester in writing explaining the refusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow current regulations for formal requirements; provide assistance to vulnerable requesters.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as adequate written reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate reasons must give a satisfactory explanation of why the decision was taken (not merely repeat empowering provisions), answer specific questions raised where possible, be in language the requester understands, and be proportionate in length to complexity/importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons need not convince the requester of correctness but must enable understanding of the decision; avoid unexplained legalese unless the requester understands technical terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasons should explain why a decision was taken, respond to specific questions, and be written in an accessible way; Part 8 of the Guide contains a detailed example of how reasons should be written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure and level of detail should match the seriousness and complexity of the decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial review purpose and available remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial review allows courts to enforce rights to just administrative action; a court can declare a decision invalid, order reconsideration, substitute its own decision, or order damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial review is a key enforcement mechanism when administrative action is unlawful, unreasonable or procedurally unfair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion of internal remedies (Section 7(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the law provides internal remedies (reviews/appeals), these must be exhausted before approaching a court for review unless exceptional circumstances/in the interests of justice are demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators should ensure affected persons are informed of internal remedies and their procedural requirements; courts may allow leave to bypass internal remedies only in exceptional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: An application for judicial review must be made within 180 days of the date on which all internal remedies were exhausted, or where there are no internal remedies, within 180 days of awareness of the decision (or when one reasonably should have become aware).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late applications will fail unless the court permits them in the interests of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — lack of authority / unlawful delegation (Section 6(2)(a)(i)-(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may review where the administrator who took the action was not authorised by the empowering provision or acted under an unauthorised delegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators must show specific legal authority for decisions; where statute requires a decision by an official of certain rank/qualification, others cannot validly take it (example: school principal's disciplinary function).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — bias (Section 6(2)(a)(iii))
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative decisions can be reviewed if the decision-maker was biased or reasonably suspected of bias (actual bias or apparent bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent bias arises where a reasonable member of the community could think the decision-maker is partial; conflicts of interest (monetary, personal interest, prejudice) commonly create apparent bias. Where bias could appear, appoint a different decision-maker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — failure to comply with mandatory and material procedure (Section 6(2)(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a mandatory and material procedure or condition prescribed by an empowering provision was not complied with, the action may be invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow procedural conditions set by empowering statutes (e.g., notice requirements before withdrawing a licence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — procedural unfairness (Section 6(2)(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to follow fair procedures (as set out in Sections 3 and 4) allows affected persons to seek a court to declare the decision invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure mandatory procedural safeguards (notice, opportunity to respond, absence of bias) are observed to avoid review on this ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — error of law (Section 6(2)(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: If administrative action was materially influenced by an error of law (a mistake about what the law requires), a court may set it aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers must understand and correctly apply the law; errors about legal requirements can invalidate decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — improper purpose, irrelevant considerations, undue dictation, bad faith, arbitrary or capricious action (Section 6(2)(e)(i)-(vi))
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions taken for reasons not authorised, for ulterior motives, because irrelevant considerations were taken into account or relevant ones ignored, because of unauthorised dictates by another person/body, in bad faith, or arbitrarily/capriciously are reviewable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use discretionary powers only for lawful purposes, consider relevant factors, do not act at the behest of others, and avoid bad faith or arbitrary decision-making. Example: town planning refusal linked to pending litigation is an improper motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — contravention of law or lack of rational connection (Section 6(2)(f)(i)-(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: An action that contravenes a law or is not rationally connected to the purpose for which it was taken, the purpose of the empowering provision, the information before the administrator, or the reasons given is reviewable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions must be rationally connected to statutory purposes and evidence; provide clear reasons showing the connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — failure to take a decision (Section 6(2)(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: An action consisting of a failure to take a decision can be reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unreasonable delay or refusal to decide when required may be challengeable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — irrationality/unreasonableness (Section 6(2)(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the exercise of power or performance of a function in pursuance of which the action was taken is so unreasonable that no reasonable person could have so acted, the action is reviewable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the classic 'no reasonable decision-maker' standard; decisions must be rational and reasonable in light of available information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for judicial review — otherwise unconstitutional or unlawful (Section 6(2)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: An administrative action that is otherwise unconstitutional or unlawful may be reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures any other forms of illegality or constitutional infirmity are catch-all grounds for review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator obligations when an action is taken to court
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide indicates administrators must know what to do when administrative action is taken to court (further detail follows in the Guide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrators should be prepared for judicial processes and ensure records, reasons, and compliance with procedures are documented; a court can make several remedial orders (invalidity, reconsideration, substitution, damages).
